title: Why That Cringe Memory Never Leaves You
description:
Why does an embarrassing moment replay in your head for years? Emotional arousal tells your brain to store an event more strongly, and replaying it locks it in even deeper. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: McGaugh (2004), 'The amygdala modulates the consolidation of memories of emotionally arousing experiences', Annual Review of Neuroscience.

#psychology #shorts #memory #brain #psychologyfacts #cognitivebias #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: Flashbulb-memory finding (Talarico & Rubin, 2003): confidence in 9/11 memories stayed high while consistency of details declined, similar to everyday memories. Emotional memories feel vivid but are not necessarily more accurate. Simplified: the amygdala works with other regions (e.g. hippocampus), not alone.

title: Nobody's Watching You As Much As You Think
description:
Think everyone noticed your slip-up? In a classic study, people wearing an embarrassing T-shirt guessed about twice as many observers would notice it as actually did. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Gilovich, Medvec & Savitsky (2000), 'The spotlight effect in social judgment', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.

#psychology #shorts #spotlighteffect #socialanxiety #confidence #psychologyfacts #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: Figures are approximate: in the original study wearers estimated roughly 46% of observers would notice the shirt, versus roughly 23% who did. The effect has been replicated across several tasks, but sizes vary.

title: The One-Cent Trick Behind Every $9.99
description:
Why does $9.99 feel so much cheaper than $10? Your brain anchors on the leftmost digit, so a one-cent change can feel like a much bigger drop. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Thomas & Morwitz (2005), 'Penny wise and pound foolish: the left-digit effect in price cognition', Journal of Consumer Research.

#psychology #shorts #pricing #marketing #shopping #psychologyfacts #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: The left-digit effect is well documented, but its strength depends on the product and context. Premium or luxury brands often use round prices because round numbers can signal quality. Thomas & Morwitz also showed that the same price difference is judged larger when it changes the leftmost digit.

title: Your Brain Hides Evidence You Disagree With
description:
Your brain naturally seeks out information that agrees with what you already believe. Peter Wason's classic 2-4-6 task shows how people test ideas in ways that can only confirm them. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Wason (1960), 'On the failure to eliminate hypotheses in a conceptual task', Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.

#psychology #shorts #confirmationbias #cognitivebias #criticalthinking #psychologyfacts #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: Wason's task is a classic demonstration of seeking confirming evidence; it is a simplified model of real-world belief formation. Confirmation bias is robust but not absolute: people can be nudged to look for disconfirming evidence.

title: Why Unfinished Tasks Haunt Your Brain
description:
Unfinished tasks can nag at your mind, but the details of the Zeigarnik effect are more nuanced than the popular story. Making a specific plan can quiet that mental nagging. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Masicampo & Baumeister (2011), 'Consider it done! Plan making can eliminate the cognitive effects of unfulfilled goals', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.

#psychology #shorts #zeigarnik #productivity #procrastination #psychologyfacts #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: The original Zeigarnik memory advantage for interrupted tasks has had inconsistent replication; the safer claim is that unfinished goals intrude on thought and that specific plans reduce this intrusion (Masicampo & Baumeister, 2011). The popular 'waiter' origin story is anecdotal.

title: Why Losing Hurts More Than Winning Feels Good
description:
Losses tend to feel bigger than equal gains, an idea called loss aversion. Researchers still debate how strong and universal it really is. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Kahneman & Tversky (1979), 'Prospect theory: an analysis of decision under risk', Econometrica.

#psychology #shorts #lossaversion #behavioraleconomics #decisionmaking #psychologyfacts #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: 'Roughly twice as large' is a common estimate (about 2 to 2.5 in Tversky & Kahneman, 1992), but some researchers (e.g. Gal & Rucker, 2018) argue loss aversion is overstated or context-dependent. The evolutionary explanation is a hypothesis, not established fact.

title: Dunning-Kruger: What Everyone Gets Wrong
description:
Do unskilled people really think they're geniuses? Not quite: Dunning and Kruger found that low performers overestimated their ability on specific tasks, but the popular version of the story is oversimplified. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Kruger & Dunning (1999), 'Unskilled and unaware of it', Journal of Personality and Social Psychology.

#psychology #shorts #dunningkruger #cognitivebias #selfawareness #psychologyfacts #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: Disputed/oversimplified: critics argue part of the classic pattern can arise from statistical effects (regression to the mean and the better-than-average effect). The popular 'Mount Stupid' curve does not appear in the original paper. The finding concerns specific skills, not general intelligence.

title: Why That Song Won't Leave Your Head
description:
Earworms often follow recent listening, stress, or a memory cue, and tend to have simple, easy-to-sing melodies. A small experiment found that chewing gum can reduce them. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Beaman, Powell & Rapley (2015), 'Want to block earworms from conscious awareness? B(u)y gum!', Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.

#psychology #shorts #earworm #music #brain #psychologyfacts #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: The 90%+ weekly figure comes from a survey of Finnish adults (Liikkanen, 2012) and may not generalize. Song traits (fairly fast tempo, simple/common melodic shapes) follow Jakubowski et al. (2016). The chewing-gum finding comes from small lab experiments and shouldn't be treated as a guaranteed cure; the research on why particular songs become earworms is still developing.

title: The Pricing Trick Stores Use on You
description:
The first number you see quietly shapes your later judgments, which is why stores show a high original price next to the sale price. This is called anchoring. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Tversky & Kahneman (1974), 'Judgment under uncertainty: heuristics and biases', Science.

#psychology #shorts #anchoring #marketing #negotiation #psychologyfacts #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: Anchoring is one of the more robust effects in judgment research, though effect sizes vary by task. Figures are medians from the original wheel-of-fortune experiment (about 25% vs about 45%). Some later 'arbitrary anchor' studies (e.g. the Social Security number version) have had mixed replication, so we stick to the classic study.

title: Why You Forget Things Walking Into a Room
description:
Walking through a doorway can make you forget why you entered the room. Researchers think doorways mark 'event boundaries' that make your brain file the old thought away. New psychology short every day on The Psyche Discourse. Source: Radvansky, Krawietz & Tamplin (2011), 'Walking through doorways causes forgetting', Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology.

#psychology #shorts #memory #doorwayeffect #brain #psychologyfacts #thepsychediscourse
accuracy_note: The doorway effect is documented in lab studies, but researchers still debate the exact mechanism (event boundaries vs. context change). Returning to the original room to restore context cues is supported by broader research on context-dependent memory, not just this study.
